title: Design a Notification Service
brief: Other teams call this service to send emails, push messages and texts to users. Requests arrive in sharp bursts, such as a marketing blast. Users can opt out, so every request checks their preferences first. The actual sending is done by an external provider that is slow and rate limited, and a message must never be delivered twice, even if a worker retries.
constraints: Accepting a send request must take under 200 ms
About 5,000 send requests per second at peak, and bursts of three times that
Opted-out users must never be messaged
A message is delivered at most once, even when a delivery is retried
Delivery goes through an external provider with a rate limit you buy by the plan
Old delivery logs are purged by a background job

capabilities.label: Accept a send request
capabilities.hint: Validate the request and record it

capabilities.label: Check preferences
capabilities.hint: Look up whether the user has opted out of this channel

capabilities.label: Deliver through the provider
capabilities.hint: Hand the message to the external provider. About 15% of requests become a real send.

capabilities.label: Purge old delivery logs
capabilities.hint: A sweep that deletes logs older than the retention period, about 300 per second

scenarios.title: Typical peak
scenarios.description: Steady send requests at the usual peak.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Which parts of sending a message must happen before you answer the caller, and which can wait?
scenarios.debrief: The API does only the quick part (validate, check preferences, enqueue) and returns; the provider's slowness is hidden behind the queue.

scenarios.title: Marketing blast (3x)
scenarios.description: A campaign triples the request rate for a few minutes.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Where does the burst pile up, and how do you keep the provider's rate limit from becoming your outage?
scenarios.debrief: Autoscaling widens the API and workers, and the queue buffers the extra sends so the provider's rate limit is respected.

scenarios.title: Delivery workers crash
scenarios.description: Whatever runs delivery loses an instance.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Workers die mid-send. How do you make sure the message goes out exactly once?
scenarios.debrief: A second worker keeps draining the queue, and idempotent handling means a retried message is not sent twice.

scenarios.title: Preference lookups slow down
scenarios.description: Whatever runs the preference check becomes 10x slower.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: You cannot skip the opt-out check. What do you do instead to keep requests fast?
scenarios.debrief: Opt-outs cannot be skipped, so preferences sit behind a cache and have their own service sized well above the request rate.

requirements.text: Requests are accepted within the latency target at peak
At least 98% of requests are accepted during the blast
Delivery is decoupled from accepting requests (queue plus worker)
The hand-off to delivery is an async connection
The design explains how opt-outs are enforced

rubric: Sending is asynchronous: the API accepts, records and queues, and workers deliver at the provider's pace.
Delivery is idempotent (a message id or a dedupe check), so a retry cannot send twice.
The opt-out check is on the request path and fast (cached preferences), and is never skipped.
The queue buffers bursts so the provider rate limit does not drop messages.
Log purging runs apart from the API servers.

reference.summary: Accept requests quickly, check opt-outs from a cache, and deliver asynchronously through idempotent workers behind a queue.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then an API Server (7 replicas, autoscale to 20, idempotency keys, circuit breaker) running 'Accept a send request'.
A Preferences Service (2 replicas) reads a Cache (90% hit) in front of the Database to check opt-outs on every request.
The API Server sends work asynchronously to a Queue (2 partitions) read by Delivery Workers (idempotent, batched, autoscale) that call a Third-party API set to Email / SMS.
A separate Worker purges old delivery logs.
tradeoffs: Asynchronous delivery turns a blast into a queue instead of errors, but messages lag while the queue drains.
Idempotent workers make retries safe at the cost of a duplicate check per message.
